title: Exact countable sums compute derived coproducts
statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category [def-sp-abelian] with exact countable direct sums: every family $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ indexed by a countable set in the chosen universe has a coproduct [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit], and taking the coproduct of any countable family of short exact sequences gives a short exact sequence. Let $Q:\mathrm{CoCh}(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal A)$ be localization at quasi-isomorphisms [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. For every countable family of unbounded cochain complexes $(K_i^\bullet)_{i\in I}$, the termwise direct sum $S^\bullet$, with $S^r=\bigoplus_iK_i^r$ and differential induced by the differentials of $K_i$, is a complex, and $Q(S^\bullet)$ with coprojections $Q(\iota_i)$ is a coproduct of the $Q(K_i^\bullet)$ in $D(\mathcal A)$. The empty family is included.

proof.text: Form $S^r=\bigoplus_i K_i^r$ in $\mathcal A$. By the coproduct universal property define $d_S^r$ by $d_S^r\iota_i^r=\iota_i^{r+1}d_i^r$. Then $d_S^{r+1}d_S^r\iota_i^r=\iota_i^{r+2}d_i^{r+1}d_i^r=0$, hence $d_S^{r+1}d_S^r=0$ for every r and each $\iota_i$ is a chain map. Degreewise assembly of a family of chain maps gives a chain map out of S, uniquely, since the chain-map equations can be checked on every coprojection. This also works in the homotopy category: representatives assemble degreewise, and component homotopies $h_i^r:K_i^r\to T^{r-1}$ assemble to $h^r:S^r\to T^{r-1}$. The homotopy equation $f-g=d_T h+h d_S$ holds if and only if it holds on all coprojections. Thus S with its coprojections is a coproduct in $K(\mathcal A)$ as well. Write $\overline Q:K(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal A)$ for the induced localization; on a chain map its value is Q of that chain map.

Exact countable sums imply the following cohomology computation, directly from the hypothesis. Put $Z_i^r=\ker d_i^r$ and $B_i^r=\operatorname{im}d_i^{r-1}$. Sum the short exact sequences $0\to Z_i^r\to K_i^r\to B_i^{r+1}\to0$ and $0\to B_i^{r+1}\to K_i^{r+1}\to K_i^{r+1}/B_i^{r+1}\to0$. Since $d_S^r$ factors through the resulting epimorphism to $\bigoplus_i B_i^{r+1}$ and its monomorphism into $S^{r+1}$, these identify $\ker d_S^r=\bigoplus_i Z_i^r$ and $\operatorname{im}d_S^{r-1}=\bigoplus_i B_i^r$. Summing $0\to B_i^r\to Z_i^r\to H^r(K_i)\to0$ now gives $H^r(S)\cong\bigoplus_i H^r(K_i)$. For a family of chain maps $c_i:K_i\to L_i$, the equalities $d_{L_i}c_i=c_i d_{K_i}$ induce maps $Z_i^r(K)\to Z_i^r(L)$ and $B_i^r(K)\to B_i^r(L)$. The summed maps commute with the summed inclusions into $S^r$ by checking each coprojection, and therefore with their quotient maps by the cokernel universal property. Thus under the displayed identification $H^r(\bigoplus_i c_i)$ is $\bigoplus_i H^r(c_i)$. Consequently a countable direct sum of quasi-isomorphisms is a quasi-isomorphism: its cohomology maps identify with sums of isomorphisms, whose inverses are the sums of the inverses. Also quasi-isomorphisms satisfy two-out-of-three, by applying each $H^r$ and two-out-of-three for isomorphisms.

For a target complex L and maps $\alpha_i:Q(K_i)\to Q(L)$, use the right calculus for quasi-isomorphisms and right-fraction representation to choose $s_i:M_i\to K_i$ quasi-isomorphisms and $f_i:M_i\to L$ in $K(\mathcal A)$ with $\alpha_i=\overline Q(f_i)\overline Q(s_i)^{-1}$. Choose chain representatives. Step 1 assembles $f:\bigoplus_i M_i\to L$ and $s=\bigoplus_i s_i:\bigoplus_i M_i\to S$; step 2 makes s a quasi-isomorphism. Define $\alpha=Q(f)Q(s)^{-1}$. For the coprojection $j_i:M_i\to\bigoplus_i M_i$, the equality $s j_i=\iota_i s_i$ gives $Q(s)^{-1}Q(\iota_i)=Q(j_i)Q(s_i)^{-1}$, hence $\alpha Q(\iota_i)=Q(f_i)Q(s_i)^{-1}=\alpha_i$. Every derived target is represented by a complex, or is isomorphic to its image under Q, so existence for these targets suffices.

We record exactly the equality criterion needed below, as a specialization of common refinement, not as an additional lemma. If $u,v:X\to Y$ in $K(\mathcal A)$ satisfy $\overline Q(u)=\overline Q(v)$, apply common refinement to the two right fractions $(1_X,u)$ and $(1_X,v)$. It supplies $a,b:N\to X$ with $1_Xa=1_Xb\in\mathrm{Qis}$ and $u a=v b$. Thus $a=b$ is a quasi-isomorphism and $u a=v a$ in the homotopy category.

For uniqueness, let $\alpha,\beta:Q(S)\to Q(L)$ have equal restrictions. Right-fraction representation gives roofs $(s_1:M_1\to S,f_1:M_1\to L)$ and $(s_2:M_2\to S,f_2:M_2\to L)$. Use the right-calculus square axiom RMS2 for $s_1$ and $s_2$: there are $u:N\to M_2$ quasi-isomorphic and $v:N\to M_1$ with $s_1v=s_2u$. The latter composite is a quasi-isomorphism by composition, and v is one by two-out-of-three from step 2. Therefore put $s=s_1v=s_2u$, $f=f_1v$, $g=f_2u$. Functoriality and cancellation of the inverted denominators give $\alpha=\overline Q(f)\overline Q(s)^{-1}$ and $\beta=\overline Q(g)\overline Q(s)^{-1}$, with a common denominator $s:N\to S$.

For each i, apply RMS2 to $s:N\to S$ and $\iota_i:K_i\to S$. It gives $t_i:P_i\to K_i$ quasi-isomorphic and $b_i:P_i\to N$ with $s b_i=\iota_i t_i$ in $K(\mathcal A)$. Consequently $\alpha Q(\iota_i)\overline Q(t_i)=\overline Q(f b_i)$ and $\beta Q(\iota_i)\overline Q(t_i)=\overline Q(g b_i)$. Equal restrictions imply equality of these two localized numerators. Step 4 supplies a quasi-isomorphism $v_i:T_i\to P_i$ with $f b_i v_i=g b_i v_i$ in $K(\mathcal A)$. Set $a_i=b_i v_i$ and $q_i=t_i v_i$. Then $s a_i=\iota_i q_i$, $f a_i=g a_i$, and $q_i$ is a quasi-isomorphism. All choices are indexed by the original countable set I.

Assemble $a:\bigoplus_i T_i\to N$ from the $a_i$ and $q:\bigoplus_i T_i\to S$ from $\iota_i q_i$, in the homotopy category by step 1. Choose chain representatives of $s,f,g,a_i,q_i$. The equalities in step 6 give degree-minus-one homotopies $h_i$ with $s a_i-\iota_i q_i=d_S h_i+h_i d_{T_i}$ and $k_i$ with $f a_i-g a_i=d_L k_i+k_i d_{T_i}$. For every r assemble $h^r:(\bigoplus_i T_i)^r\to S^{r-1}$ and $k^r:(\bigoplus_i T_i)^r\to L^{r-1}$. Checking each coprojection gives $s a-q=d_S h+h d_{\bigoplus T_i}$ and $f a-g a=d_L k+k d_{\bigoplus T_i}$. Hence $s a=q$ and $f a=g a$ in $K(\mathcal A)$. Step 2 says q is a quasi-isomorphism. Hence a is a quasi-isomorphism by two-out-of-three, since s is one. Applying the localization to $f a=g a$ and cancelling the invertible $\overline Q(a)$ proves $\overline Q(f)=\overline Q(g)$, and therefore $\alpha=\beta$. This fills the uniqueness verification omitted by Tag 0A5L.

Existence in step 3 and uniqueness in steps 4–7 give exactly the coproduct universal property for $Q(S)$ and the specified $Q(\iota_i)$. For $I=\varnothing$, degreewise coproducts in $\mathcal A$ are zero objects, S is the zero complex, and assembly in step 1 gives a unique homotopy-class map out of S. In steps 3 and 7 the empty sums s and q are the unique maps between the chosen zero complexes. Their degreewise inverses are the unique maps in the reverse direction, since each composite is the unique endomorphism of a zero object and hence its identity. Thus s and q are quasi-isomorphisms and the existence and cancellation arguments apply. Thus the empty coproduct is included, without a boundedness hypothesis.
